title: mTOR Pathway: From Cellular Physiology to Clinical Practice
abstract:
## The Physiology of mTOR  
mTOR functions in two main protein complexes:  
- **mTORC1**: Responds to nutrients, growth factors, and energy availability. Promotes protein synthesis, lipid production, and cell proliferation. Inhibits autophagy (cellular “recycling”).
- **mTORC2**: Regulates cell survival, cytoskeleton organization, and insulinsignaling. Plays a role in glucose and lipid metabolism.  
**Activation signals include:**  
- Amino acids, especially branched-chain amino acids ([BCAAs](https://gertitashkomd.com/services-bcaas-insulin-and-metabolic-health-helpful-or-harmful/))
- [Insulin](https://gertitashkomd.com/the-role-of-insulin/)and IGF-1
- Cellular energy abundance (high ATP)  
**Inhibition signals include:**  
- Nutrient deprivation
- Low energy states (high AMP/ATP ratio)
- Stress hormones and hypoxia  
This tight regulation ensures that mTOR responds appropriately to changing internal and external conditions.
## mTOR Across the Lifespan  
In youth, mTOR activity supports growth, muscle building, and repair. In adulthood, sustained high mTOR activity, driven by excess calories, constant nutrient intake, and insulin resistance, can promote metabolic strain. In later life, overactivation is linked to aging, inflammation, and certain cancers.
### 3. PCOS and Hormonal Imbalance  
In PCOS, nutrient and insulin signaling abnormalities can cause unbalanced mTOR activation in ovarian tissue, influencing follicular development and androgen production. Tailoring diet and exercise can help recalibrate this pathway.
